q: Which of these is outside a certified personal trainer's scope of practice?
o: Diagnosing the cause of a client's knee pain
e: Diagnosing and treating areas of pain or disease sits with medical professionals. A CPT assesses, programmes, gives general nutritional information and refers out for anything beyond that.

q: How is a fitness professional's scope of practice mainly defined in the US?
o: By federal legislation specific to personal trainers
By the certifying body alone, with no legal weight
Through association to adjacent allied health professions, whose rules prohibit certain activities
e: There is no specific governmental regulation for fitness professionals in the US and many other countries. The boundary comes from adjacent professions, whose own rules stop CPTs doing certain health-related activities.

q: Nutrition counselling is:
o: Never permitted to anyone but a doctor
Reserved for a registered dietitian nutritionist in some regions and unlicensed in others
Within scope provided the client signs a disclaimer
e: Scope varies by country and region. In some places only a registered dietitian nutritionist may counsel on nutrition; in others no licence is required. You must know current local law.

q: Which certification must a CPT hold current and be able to act on in an emergency?
e: Holding current CPR and AED certification, and responding appropriately in emergencies, is explicitly within scope and expected of the professional.

q: Under the NASM Code of Professional Conduct, which belongs to the 'honesty, integrity and lawfulness' area?
o: Maintaining a hygienic and professional appearance
Carrying adequate liability insurance and keeping progress notes for each client
Storing and disposing of records securely
e: That area covers liability insurance, progress notes for each client, truthful and dignified advertising, accurate financial records and compliance with harassment and discrimination law.

q: What can follow a failure to comply with the Code of Professional Conduct?
o: A mandatory retake of the written exam
Revocation of the certification, and in serious cases legal action
A fine paid to the certifying body
e: The stated consequence is the certification being revoked, with legal action possible in serious cases.

q: A client says 'I feel like everyone is staring at me.' Which barrier is this?
e: Social physique anxiety is anxiety about physical appearance, or about how the client believes others see and judge them. Responses include comfortable clothing, quieter areas and alternative ways to participate.

q: Which barrier is described as the largest, used to explain lack of exercise, poor eating and poor stress management alike?
e: Time is the largest barrier. The approach is to find where there is genuinely no wiggle room and design around it, often placing exercise first thing in the morning or immediately after work.

q: Why does an unrealistic goal itself become a barrier?
o: It takes too long to write down
The client believes they are not making progress, feels defeated and stops
It requires equipment the client lacks
e: Clients get too ambitious, then frustrated. Believing they are not progressing leads to feeling defeated and stopping, so goals need flexibility, progression and celebrated milestones.

q: A client appears not to care about starting. What is the likely root cause?
e: Ambivalence looks like not caring but the root cause is mixed feelings. The response is to talk through the benefits of exercise and the negative effects of sedentary living.

q: Convenience as a barrier is best described as:
o: Objective and measurable in travel minutes
Entirely subjective; clients accept inconvenience if they believe the value is exceptional
e: Convenience is entirely subjective. Clients will accept inconvenience where they believe they are getting exceptional value, and options include home, lunch hour or between-activity exercise.

q: Believing you lack the time or energy is which type of barrier?
o: A barrier of perception, which may genuinely feel physical to the client
e: Barriers are physical, perceptual or mixed. A perceived barrier can feel entirely physical to the person experiencing it, so it should not be dismissed.

q: In the study cited, gym members who predicted three or more sessions a week actually averaged:
e: People overestimate how often they will exercise. Predicted three or more, achieved an average of 1.39 a week.

q: 'I will always work out during my lunch break' is an example of:
e: Implementation intentions drive behaviour by identifying cues towards action. Coping planning is the separate technique of anticipating barriers and creating alternative plans.

q: Which cognitive strategy involves saying 'stop' out loud when negative thought patterns appear?
e: The stopping technique breaks the cycle of negative thinking. Reverse listing is the complementary one: identify the negative inner narrative and replace it with positive statements.

q: A client mentally rehearses a session focusing on making their technique as close to perfect as possible. This is:
e: Mental imagery has three subsets: appearance imagery (appearance or health outcomes), energy imagery (energy and stress relief) and technique imagery (focus on technique).

q: When does positive feedback and praise matter most for building self-efficacy?
o: In the early stages of behaviour change
Once the client reaches their outcome goal
e: Praise on any improvement in any metric builds confidence through little victories, and it matters most in the early stages of behaviour change.

q: For a client in the contemplation stage, serious planning may be premature. What is suggested instead?
o: Setting a demanding outcome goal to create urgency
Reviewing barriers that have already arisen and collaborating on plans for their recurrence
Postponing all conversation until they act
e: Timing matters. In contemplation it is better to review barriers already experienced and plan together for when they recur.

q: What is the stated primary goal of the fitness professional?
o: To help individuals adopt a regular exercise programme and stay active for the long term
To retain clients for as many sessions as possible
e: Adoption plus long-term maintenance. That is why understanding how ready a client is to change matters so much.

q: In NASM's wording, SMART stands for:
e: NASM uses Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic, Timely. Failing any one criterion means the goal will likely fail to meet the client's needs.

q: 'Win a 10K race within one year' is which kind of goal?
e: An outcome goal is the consequence, the final achievement. Process goals are the daily and weekly steps, such as jogging an hour three days a week.

q: Why do process goals enhance self-efficacy?
o: They are easier to measure than outcome goals
They remove the need for an outcome goal
They are set by the trainer rather than the client
e: Once an outcome goal is set, process goals should be created that speak to how it will be achieved, and each small win on them builds confidence.

q: What distinguishes 'Attainable' from 'Realistic' in NASM's SMART?
o: Attainable concerns the level of challenge; Realistic concerns relevance to this client's actual life
Attainable concerns time; Realistic concerns measurement
Attainable applies to outcome goals only
e: Too easy and the client will not put in sufficient effort; too challenging and they get discouraged. Realistic asks whether it is possible for this client's lifestyle, not just technically possible.

q: Goals sit at the crossroads of how and why. What is the 'why'?
e: The why is the client's values; the how is the way the goal will be achieved. Both professional and client should be able to verbalise why a goal matters.

q: When should goal setting begin?
o: At the first meeting, focused on long-term goals based on personal values
e: It starts at the first meeting. Useful questions are 'What do you want to accomplish in the next six months?' and 'What does success in fitness look like to you?'

q: What does the PAR-Q+ answer?
o: Whether it is safe for them to become more physically active
What their body fat percentage is
e: The PAR-Q+ is the pre-participation health screen: it answers safety. The Lifestyle and Health History Questionnaire answers who the person is. They are used together.

q: How many general health questions does the PAR-Q+ (2024) contain?
e: Seven general questions. All 'no' means the client is cleared and signs the participant declaration. Any 'yes' routes to follow-up pages on specific chronic conditions.

q: A client answers 'yes' to a PAR-Q+ question. What happens?
o: They are routed to follow-up pages on specific chronic conditions, which can require medical clearance or referral
The trainer decides on the spot
e: Follow-up pages address specific chronic conditions and can require medical clearance or referral before starting.

q: Which section of the Lifestyle and Health History Questionnaire covers extended sitting, repetitive movements and heeled footwear?
e: The Occupation section captures the job itself plus extended sitting, repetitive movements and heeled footwear, all of which shape posture.

q: Which pulse site should be avoided when measuring a client's resting heart rate?
e: Reaching for a client's neck causes discomfort and spikes the reading, pressure can occlude blood flow to the brain, and it can induce a vasovagal response producing a large drop in heart rate and blood pressure.

q: Why should you never take a pulse with your thumb?
o: It is too short to reach the artery
It has a strong pulse of its own, so you risk counting yours
It is less sensitive than the fingers
It compresses the artery too hard
e: The thumb has a strong pulse of its own and is more sensitive. Use the first and second finger instead.

q: What is the best method for obtaining resting heart rate?
o: Immediately after the first training session
First thing in the morning, taken by the client after sitting up out of bed, ideally a three or five day average
At the end of a warm-up
Any time the client is seated for five minutes
e: First thing in the morning, self-taken after sitting up, averaged over three or five days. Wearable continuous heart rate devices are relatively accurate and acceptable.

q: Which counting duration gives the most accurate resting heart rate?
e: A full 60 seconds is most accurate. The shorter the count, the greater the error introduced by multiplying up.

q: What does the systolic number measure?
o: Force on the vessel walls between heartbeats
Force on the vessel walls when the heart contracts
The volume of blood pumped per minute
e: Systolic, the top number, is the force when the heart contracts. Diastolic, the bottom number, is the force between heartbeats as blood returns to the heart.

q: What are Korotkoff sounds?
o: The sound of the cuff inflating
The sound blood makes bouncing off the vessel walls, heard through the stethoscope
e: They are what you hear through the stethoscope. The first prominent sound is systolic, the last sound before silence is diastolic.

q: At what rate should cuff pressure be released when taking blood pressure?
e: Release slowly, about 2 mmHg per second, having inflated above the expected systolic, around 150 to 160 mmHg.

q: Where should blood pressure be measured, and why?
o: At the wrist, because it is most convenient
Level with the heart, because pressure differs with body position
Above the head, to reduce the reading
At the ankle, for a peripheral measure
e: Measure level with the heart, using the left upper arm rested on a box or desk, because pressure differs with body position.

q: Normal blood pressure is defined as:
e: Under 120 systolic and under 80 diastolic. Elevated measurements are hypertension, which has stages depending on how elevated.

q: Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Peripheral resistance increases when the arteries are:
e: Constricted arteries increase peripheral resistance; dilated arteries decrease it.

q: A resting heart rate below 60 bpm is called:
e: Bradycardia is below 60, tachycardia is above 100, and the untrained adult range is approximately 60 to 100 bpm.

q: Stroke volume is calculated as:
o: Cardiac output divided by heart rate squared
e: End-diastolic volume is the filled volume before contraction; end-systolic volume is the residual after ejection. Typical adult stroke volume is roughly 75 to 80 mL per beat.

q: A well-conditioned client has a slower than normal resting heart rate. Why?
o: The training improved the heart's ability to pump blood
They have less blood in total
e: Conditioning improves the heart's pumping ability, so fewer beats are needed at rest.

q: Which body fat measurement method is the gold standard?
e: Hydrostatic weighing is the gold standard and most body-fat-and-health charts were produced with it, but it is expensive and typically found in university settings.

q: The main source of inaccuracy in bioelectrical impedance is:
e: BIA gives a good indication but depends heavily on hydration, which is why it is less reliable than the reference methods.

q: Skinfold calipers carry roughly what error against hydrostatic weighing?
e: About 3.5%, and the inaccuracy is mostly user error, which means practice reduces it. That makes calipers practical in a fitness setting.

q: What is the most common error in taking a skinfold measurement?
o: Grabbing a small pinch of skin instead of gripping the fat and pulling it away from the muscle
e: Get a good grip on the fat and pull it away from the muscle, spreading your fingers two to three inches apart. Place the calipers just below your fingers, then remove your fingers before reading.

q: How soon should you read the calipers after releasing pressure?
e: Read within one to two seconds. Leaving the calipers on compresses the fat and changes the reading. Wait at least 15 seconds before repeating a site.

q: Two consecutive measurements at a skinfold site must agree within:
e: Within one to two millimetres, otherwise repeat until they do.

q: In the three-site skinfold protocol for men, which sites are used?
e: Men: chest (diagonal), abdomen (vertical), thigh (vertical). Women: triceps (vertical), suprailiac (diagonal), thigh (vertical).

q: Which fold direction is correct for the male chest site?
e: The male chest fold is diagonal, halfway between the crease of the armpit and the nipple. The abdomen and thigh folds are vertical.

q: Waist-to-hip ratio is calculated as:
o: Hip circumference divided by waist circumference
Waist circumference divided by hip circumference
e: Waist divided by hips. An apple shape, where the waist measures larger than the hips, is associated with negative health risks because more fat is distributed around the organs.

q: Where is the waist measured for waist-to-hip ratio?
o: At the level of the umbilicus
At the most narrow part of the torso
e: The most narrow part of the torso, found with the client standing with arms out. The hips are measured at the area of largest circumference, taking the buttocks into account.

q: When during the breath should the waist measurement be taken?
o: At the end of the breath, after the client breathes in and releases
e: Have them breathe in and release, then measure at the end of the breath. Use a non-elastic tape pulled snug but not too tight.

q: What are the five kinetic chain checkpoints?
o: Foot and ankle, knee, LPHC, shoulders, head and neck
e: Foot and ankle, knee, LPHC, shoulders, head and neck, each checked from three views: anterior, posterior and lateral.

q: The output of a static postural assessment is not a list of observations but three judgements. What are they?
o: Evidence of a postural distortion syndrome, which muscles are potentially overactive, and which are potentially underactive
Range of motion at three joints
e: The point is to reach conclusions, not record findings: is there a distortion syndrome, which muscles are potentially overactive, which are potentially underactive.

q: Flat feet with adducted and internally rotated knees, giving a knock-kneed appearance, describes which distortion pattern?
e: That is the lower-extremity pattern. Stretch the calves and adductor complex; strengthen the foot and ankle stabilisers (anterior tibialis) and the gluteals.

q: In the LPHC distortion pattern, which muscles are stretched and which strengthened?
o: Stretch hip flexors, strengthen gluteals and core
e: Sitting leaves the hip flexors shortened and tight and the gluteals and deep core lengthened and weak. Stretch the hip flexors, strengthen the gluteals and deep abdominals.

q: What is the practical tell for anterior pelvic tilt?
o: The belt line, higher at the back and lower at the front
The position of the shoulder blades
Head position relative to the wall
e: A belt line higher at the back and lower at the front indicates anterior tilt, which comes with a hyperextended lower back, also called excessive lumbar lordosis.

q: Rounded shoulders and upper back with a forward head produces:
e: That is the upper-extremity pattern, common in people who sit at a computer or drive for long periods. It can cause shoulder pain, neck pain and headaches.

q: In the upper-extremity pattern, what should be strengthened?
o: Middle back (rhomboids, mid and lower trapezius) and shoulder stabilisers (rotator cuff)
e: Stretch the chest and upper trapezius; strengthen the middle back and rotator cuff. The logic throughout: what is held short becomes overactive and needs stretching, what is held long becomes underactive and needs strengthening.

q: Why is a static postural assessment alone incomplete?
o: Posture is dynamic and constantly adjusts to the body's demands
e: Posture adjusts constantly, so a dynamic test is needed. The overhead squat assessment is usually the first dynamic test and acts as a total body scan.

q: What does the OHSA evaluate in one movement?
o: Dynamic posture, core stability, flexibility and whole-body coordination
e: All four at once, which is why it is a total body scan. Impairments it reveals, such as knee valgus or limited ankle mobility, can predict injury risk and direct the programme.

q: What is the correct starting position for the OHSA?
o: Feet hip-width, shoes on, hands on hips
Feet shoulder-width pointing straight, barefoot, arms overhead with elbows straight
Feet wide and turned out, arms crossed
Feet together, arms by the sides
e: Feet shoulder-width and pointing straight on a flat surface, feet and ankles neutral, barefoot so the foot and ankle are visible, arms overhead with straight elbows.

q: How many repetitions are performed, and from which views?
o: Five, observed from the front and from the side
e: Five repetitions, squatting to thighs parallel and returning, modifying depth if needed, observed anteriorly and laterally.

q: Arms falling forward during the overhead squat indicates:
o: Weakness in the front of the shoulder
Overactivity in the front of the shoulder and weakness across the shoulder blades, upper back and posterior shoulder
e: Ideally the arms stay vertical as an extension of the torso with the biceps by the ears. The fix is flexibility through the front and activation and strengthening through the upper back.

q: What is the ideal relationship between shin and torso in the lateral view of an overhead squat?
o: The torso vertical regardless of the shin
The shin vertical regardless of the torso
e: A parallel line between shin and torso. Excessive forward lean suggests weakness in the spinal muscles, spinal column and hips, with possible overactivity in the front of the hip.

q: How is knee buckling judged?
o: By the middle of the kneecaps falling inside the big toes
e: Middle of the kneecaps falling inside the big toes. It indicates overactivity in the inner thigh and weakness in the outer hip.

q: What is the corrective approach for knees buckling in?
o: Strengthen the inner thigh and stretch the outer hip
Strengthen the outer hip complex, plus foam rolling and static flexibility for the inner thigh
e: Overactive gets flexibility and self-myofascial work, underactive gets activation and strengthening. Here that means adductor release and outer hip strengthening.

q: How should OHSA findings be communicated to a client?
o: As a list of faults to correct
Tactfully, framed around movement safety and efficiency rather than what is wrong with them
Not at all, to avoid discouragement
e: Tact matters. Frame the conversation around movement safety and efficiency, not around what is wrong with the client.

q: The YMCA 3-minute step test is scored on:
o: Recovery heart rate against age and sex norms
e: Recovery heart rate, rated on a seven-point scale from very poor to excellent. A lower recovery heart rate is better.

q: What are the three components of the human movement system?
e: The nervous system controls the muscles, the muscular system moves, the skeletal system determines how the joints move. Nerves move muscles; muscles move bones.

q: What is a muscle imbalance?
o: A less than optimal length-tension relationship, with one muscle short and overactive and its opposite lengthened and underactive
Any asymmetry between left and right
e: The short, overactive muscle has too much tone and pulls the bones toward its side; the lengthened, underactive one allows it. The joint then sits in a less than optimal position, increasing stress.

q: What does regional interdependence mean?
o: Joints depend on other joints for movement
The body depends on external support
e: Joints depend on other joints. Human movement system dysfunction is a stack of dominoes: an imbalance in one area tends to create imbalances throughout.

q: In the domino chain from the ground up, subtalar pronation and a collapsed arch lead first to:
e: Collapsed arch, then internal tibial rotation, then femoral rotation, then that hip drops and internally rotates, and what happens at the hip also happens at the shoulders.

q: Which is NOT one of the five functions of the skeletal system?
o: Providing the structure from which movement is created
e: The five are: shape and form, support and protection of organs, structure for movement, blood production, mineral storage.

q: Which division of the skeleton contains the skull, rib cage and vertebral column?
e: The axial skeleton has approximately 80 bones. The appendicular has approximately 126: arms, legs and pelvic girdle.

q: Which cells break down and remove old bone tissue?
e: Osteoclasts break down and remove; osteoblasts form new bone tissue. Together that is remodeling.

q: The patella is an example of which bone type?
e: Sesamoid bones are small and embedded in a joint capsule or where a tendon passes over a joint. Carpals are short, vertebrae irregular, the sternum flat, the femur long.

q: A groove allowing soft tissue such as muscle, tendon or ligament to pass through is a:
e: A sulcus is a groove and a fossa is a flattened or indented portion; both are depressions. Processes are projections where tendons and ligaments attach.

q: Trochanters are found at the top of which bone?
e: Trochanters sit at the top of the femur and are attachment sites for hip musculature. Tubercles sit at the top of the humerus for shoulder musculature.

q: Total peak bone mass is reached at approximately what age?
e: Peak bone mass is reached around 30, stays stable from 30 to 50, then declines, which is why osteoporosis risk rises in older individuals.

q: Which pair is NOT weight-bearing exercise?
e: Swimming and cycling still build muscle and cardiovascular health, and contraction force across bones carries some benefit, but they do not force the body to work against gravity.

q: Approximately what proportion of the body's joints are synovial?
e: About 80 percent, and they have the greatest capacity for motion. They are characterised by the absence of fibrous or cartilaginous tissue directly connecting the bones.

q: What does synovial fluid do?
o: Lubricates the joint surfaces and nourishes the cartilage cells lining the joint
e: It resembles egg white and works like engine oil, secreted within the capsule from the synovial membrane. It reduces excessive wear and feeds the cartilage cells.

q: The elbow and knee are which type of synovial joint?
e: Hinge joints are uniaxial, moving predominantly in one direction like a door hinge. The knee is a modified hinge, because it can slide and then roll.

q: Which joint type is the most mobile, moving in all three directions?
e: Ball-and-socket joints, the shoulder and the hip, are the most mobile. Gliding joints are non-axial and the simplest, moving back and forth or side to side.

q: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is which type?
e: In a saddle joint one bone resembles a saddle and the other straddles it like a rider, giving back-and-forth and side-to-side movement with limited rotation.

q: Which two proteins make up ligaments, and what does each contribute?
o: Actin for strength and myosin for recoil
Collagen for tensile strength and elastin for flexibility and elastic recoil
Keratin for strength and elastin for recoil
Collagen for recoil and elastin for tensile strength
e: Collagen gives the ability to withstand tension; elastin gives flexibility and elastic recoil to withstand bending and twisting. The ACL is meagre in elastin and predominantly collagen.

q: Ligaments heal slowly. Why?
e: Poor vascularity, which is also true of tendons. Both are slower to repair and adapt. Ligaments also provide sensory input to the nervous system that aids proprioception.

q: What is the difference between osteokinematics and arthrokinematics?
o: Osteokinematics is joint movement we cannot see; arthrokinematics is bone movement we can see
Osteokinematics is how the bones move, the visible vocabulary of flexion and extension; arthrokinematics is what happens inside the joint
They are two words for the same thing
Osteokinematics applies only to synovial joints
e: Osteokinematics is the visible movement, arthrokinematics is the invisible movement within the joint. Both are necessary for normal movement.

q: Which arthrokinematic motion is described as a tire rolling on the street?
e: Roll. Slide, or glide, is a bicycle tire skidding; spin is twisting the lid off a jar, as in forearm pronation and supination. Use three motions, not four.

q: Which vertebrae are the largest bones in the spinal column?
e: The lumbar vertebrae, L1 to L5, support most of the body's weight and attach to many back muscles. That is also why the lumbar spine is often a location of pain.

q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there, and what distinguishes them?
o: Twelve, each articulating with a rib
e: T1 to T12, each articulating with a rib to form the rear anchor of the rib cage. They are larger than cervical vertebrae and increase in size top to bottom.

q: What do intervertebral discs do?
o: Act as shock absorbers and allow the spine to move
e: They are fibrous cartilage sitting between the vertebrae, absorbing shock and permitting movement.

q: Neutral spine is best defined as:
o: The position in which the vertebrae and associated structures are under the least load and can most optimally support functional movement
The position of the spine when lying supine
e: Viewed from the side the spinal column is curved, partially resembling an S. The optimal arrangement of those curves is neutral spine: least load, best support for functional movement.

q: The oblique is ___ to the rectus abdominis.
e: Lateral means toward the outside of the body, medial near the middle. So the oblique is lateral to the rectus abdominis, and the rectus abdominis is medial to the oblique.

q: Which term means positioned on the opposite side of the body?
e: Contralateral is opposite side, ipsilateral is same side. Proximal is nearest the centre or point of reference, distal is farthest.

q: Lying face down on the belly, as in a plank or Superman, is:
e: Prone is face down. Supine is lying on the spine, face up, as in a crunch or bench press.

q: Biomechanics is defined as:
o: The study of muscle contraction only
The scientific study of internal or external forces placed upon the body, using the principles of physics
e: It uses the principles of physics to study how forces interact within a living body.

q: Which motions occur in the sagittal plane?
e: The sagittal plane bisects the body into left and right halves and carries flexion and extension. Sagittal means arrow.

q: The frontal plane bisects the body into which halves, and carries which motions?
o: Left and right; flexion and extension
Front and back; abduction, adduction, lateral flexion, eversion and inversion
e: Also called the coronal plane, named for the coronal suture of the skull. It carries abduction, adduction, lateral flexion, eversion and inversion.

q: Which motions belong to the transverse plane?
o: Rotation, horizontal abduction and adduction, pronation and supination
e: The transverse plane bisects the body into top and bottom halves. Transverse means across.

q: Flexion is defined as:
o: A movement away from the midline
A bending movement in which the relative angle between two adjacent segments decreases
A movement that increases the angle between segments
e: Flexion decreases the relative angle, extension increases it. Both occur at the spine, shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, foot and hand.

q: Bringing the top of the foot closer to the shin is:
e: Dorsal is the upper side, so dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot. Plantar is the sole, so plantar flexion points the foot away.

q: Hip flexion occurs two ways. The hip hinge is which?
o: Pelvis on femur, femur static and the hips moving over the top
Neither; the hip hinge is extension
e: Femur on pelvis means the hips stay still and the femur moves. Pelvis on femur, the hip hinge, means the femur stays still and the hips move over the top. Both decrease the femur-pelvis angle.

q: What is hyperextension?
o: Extension of a joint beyond the normal limit, which could result in injury
e: The term is reserved for movements where normal extension values have been exceeded.

q: Eversion of the foot is:
o: Lifting the medial portion and standing on the lateral edge
Collapsing the arch and standing more on the inside, medial portion of the foot
e: Eversion collapses the arch onto the medial portion, equivalently lifting the lateral portion off the floor. Inversion is the opposite: lifting the medial portion and standing on the lateral edge.

q: Turning the forearm from palm down to palm up is:
e: Radioulnar supination goes palm down to palm up; pronation goes palm up to palm down. Radioulnar refers to the radius and ulna.

q: A chest fly starts with the elbows out wide and moves them inward. Which motion is that?
e: Horizontal adduction moves the arm horizontally from lateral toward anterior. Do not confuse it with pressing motions using shoulder flexion and extension, which are sagittal and keep the elbows close to the torso.

q: With the feet planted, rotating the hips to the right produces:
o: External rotation of the right hip and internal rotation of the left
External rotation of the left hip and internal rotation of the right
e: Rotating right externally rotates the left hip and internally rotates the right. Rotating left reverses it.

q: Pronation of the foot and ankle complex combines:
o: Inversion, plantar flexion and forefoot adduction
Eversion, plantar flexion and forefoot adduction
e: Pronation is eversion (frontal), dorsiflexion (sagittal) and forefoot abduction (transverse). Supination is the mirror: inversion, plantar flexion, forefoot adduction.

q: In walking and running, which phase involves pronation?
o: Force production, as the foot pushes off
e: Pronation happens during force reduction, supination during force production as the foot pushes off.

q: Isolated scapular movements are called translations because:
o: They occur in two planes at once
They do not rotate around a fixed axis
They are too small to measure
e: Retraction brings the shoulder blades closer together, protraction moves them apart, elevation moves them toward the ears, depression moves them downward.

q: Why is walking a multiplanar movement?
o: The arms swing in the frontal plane
The hips, knees and ankles work sagittally while the torso works transversely, because power is generated by rotating
The head moves in three directions
e: Sagittal below, transverse above. Training across all three planes prevents imbalances; a lunge with rotation is a multiplanar training example.

q: Which are the three types of muscle tissue?
e: Cardiac and smooth make up the heart and internal organ tissues. Skeletal muscle matters most for a fitness professional.

q: The muscular system links which two systems?
e: It generates internal tension that, under the nervous system's control, manipulates the bones to produce movement.

q: Which layer of connective tissue directly surrounds an entire muscle?
o: Epimysium, also called the deep fascia
e: From outside in: fascia, epimysium (whole muscle), perimysium (each fascicle), endomysium (individual fibres), sarcolemma (the fibre's plasma membrane).

q: What is the functional unit of the muscular system?
e: The sarcomere is the repeating section of overlapping myofilaments and the physical site of contraction. Its meeting point is the Z line.

q: Actin and myosin are, respectively:
o: The thick and the thin filament
The thin and the thick filament
Two names for the same filament
e: Actin is the thin filament, myosin the thick. Sliding filament theory says they slide past one another to shorten the sarcomere and the muscle.

q: What is a motor unit?
o: One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it stimulates
e: The neuromuscular junction is where the nerve joins the muscle fibre, and the small gap there is the synapse.

q: In excitation-contraction coupling, which neurotransmitter crosses the synapse?
e: Acetylcholine is released into the junction to help the impulse cross. Sodium and potassium facilitate the impulse travelling down the neuron.

q: What does the sarcoplasmic reticulum release to trigger contraction?
e: The impulse travels into the muscle and stimulates the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium, which triggers the chain of events resulting in myosin heads binding to actin.

q: What provides the energy for the power stroke?
e: ATP powers the myosin heads pulling actin toward the sarcomere centre. After the power stroke the myosin detach and return to resting length.

q: What is the primary purpose of small motor units?
o: Moving the body, as in running and jumping
Stabilising the body, as in upright posture
e: Small motor units are fatigue resistant, contain Type I fibres, produce small forces slowly and primarily stabilise. Large motor units contain Type II fibres and move the body.

q: What does the all-or-nothing principle state?
o: A muscle either contracts fully or tears
If an impulse triggers an action potential it spreads through all the fibres of that nerve; motor units cannot vary their force
Every muscle in the body fires together
Contraction strength depends on the size of the muscle alone
e: Because motor units contract all the way or not at all, overall contraction strength depends on which type of motor unit is recruited and how many are activated.

q: Which is true of Type I fibres?
o: Smaller, red, more capillaries and mitochondria, more fatigue resistant
Fast to produce tension and quick to fatigue
e: Type I are slow-twitch, red because of myoglobin, with higher oxidative capacity. Type II are fast-twitch, white, larger and fatigue quickly.

q: Why are Type I fibres red?
o: More blood vessels on the surface
Myoglobin, similar to haemoglobin, the red oxygen-carrying pigment
e: Myoglobin is the oxygen-binding pigment in the sarcoplasm. All muscles contain varying combinations of both fibre types, depending on the muscle's function and on genetics.

q: After age 50, muscle mass is lost at an average rate of:
e: Peak mass, power and strength occur between 20 and 30, change little from 30 to 50, then decline by 1 to 2 percent a year. Resistance training is highly beneficial against this.

q: A muscle exerting less force than is placed on it, lengthening under control, is performing which action?
e: Eccentric action is synonymous with deceleration, and is often called the negative. Landing from a jump is eccentric.

q: Isometric action means:
o: The muscle exerts force equal to that placed on it, with no appreciable change in length
e: Also called dynamic stabilisation. The rotator cuff holding the shoulder during a push-up is isometric.

q: Concentric action is synonymous with:
e: Concentric means exerting more force than is placed on the muscle, so it shortens. Eccentric is deceleration, isometric is dynamic stabilisation.

q: Why train the entire muscle-action spectrum rather than emphasising concentric work?
o: It maximises strength potential, maintains joint range of motion and prevents injury
e: Traditional routines emphasise concentric production. Training all three actions gives the fuller benefit.

q: A muscle's role as agonist, synergist, stabiliser or antagonist depends on:
o: The joint motion happening at the moment
e: Roles switch. The infraspinatus is an agonist for shoulder external rotation, a synergist when the shoulder reaches overhead, and a stabiliser during other shoulder motions.

q: Which muscle is the agonist for hip extension?
e: Gluteus maximus is the prime mover for hip extension; the hamstrings act as synergist. The hip flexor complex is the antagonist.

q: In a squat, which muscle acts as the stabiliser in NASM's table?
e: Transversus abdominis stabilises the spine. In the same table the agonists are gluteus maximus and quadriceps, the synergist is the hamstrings and the antagonist is the psoas.

q: How does a stabiliser contract?
o: Isometrically, to support the joint while the movers work
e: Isometric contraction holds the joint. Examples are transversus abdominis in a squat or overhead press and the rotator cuff in a push-up.

q: In a chest press, which muscle is the antagonist?
e: Pectoralis major is the agonist, anterior deltoid and triceps the synergists, rotator cuff the stabiliser, posterior deltoid the antagonist.

q: What is feed-forward activation?
o: Contracting harder as fatigue sets in
Some muscles stabilising a joint by contracting automatically in anticipation of movement
e: Anticipatory stabilisation. It is one reason muscles rarely work in isolation but in groups controlled by the nervous system.

q: In the body, what plays the role of the fulcrum?
e: The joint axis is the fulcrum, the bones are levers, the muscles create the effort, and the resistance is body weight or an external object.

q: A biceps curl is which class of lever?
e: Third class has the effort in the middle: elbow fulcrum, biceps effort, dumbbell load. Most limbs are third class, and the effort must exceed the resistance.

q: A calf raise, with the ball of the foot as fulcrum, is which class of lever?
o: Second, like a wheelbarrow, with the resistance in the middle
Third, with the effort in the middle
e: Second class puts the resistance in the middle. A full-body push-up is the other example given. First class puts the fulcrum in the middle, as in nodding the head.

q: Why can muscles only pull, never push?
o: They are attached at only one end
Contraction shortens the muscle, so joint motion comes from muscles pulling on bones
e: The musculoskeletal system is a series of levers and pulleys, and all joint motion comes from muscles pulling on bones.

q: Which part of the neuron transmits impulses to other neurons or to effector sites?
e: The axon is the cylindrical projection carrying impulses out. Dendrites gather information from other structures; the cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and controls the cell.

q: What are the four primary electrolytes needed for proper nerve function?
e: Electrolytes are minerals carrying an electrical charge. Neurons signal both electrically and chemically.

q: Walking from pavement onto sand and changing your walking pattern uses which two nervous system functions in sequence?
o: Sensory then motor, with integrative in between
e: Sensory senses the change, integrative analyses and interprets it, motor produces the neuromuscular response.

q: The peripheral nervous system consists of:
o: 12 cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves, and sensory receptors
e: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nerves both activate effector sites (motor) and relay information back (sensory).

q: Afferent pathways carry information:
o: Down from the CNS to the muscles
Up to the CNS; they are sensory
e: Afferent is sensory, going up. Efferent is motor, going down. Interneurons transmit between them and exist only within the spinal cord and brain.

q: Which sensory receptor type relates most to the science of human movement?
e: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical forces, touch and pressure, making them the most important for a fitness professional. Nociceptors respond to pain, chemoreceptors to smell and taste, photoreceptors to light.

q: Muscle spindles run parallel to the muscle fibres and are sensitive to:
o: Muscular tension and its rate of change
Muscle length and the rate of length change
e: They regulate contraction through the stretch reflex mechanism, returning a contract response within 1 to 2 milliseconds to protect the muscle from stretching too far or too fast.

q: What happens when a Golgi tendon organ is activated?
e: GTOs sit where skeletal muscle fibres insert into the tendons and sense change in muscular tension and its rate. Activation causes the muscle to relax, preventing excessive stress and possible injury.

q: Joint receptors signal:
e: They sit in and around the joint capsule, respond to pressure, acceleration and deceleration, and act as another automatic safeguard against injury.

q: Proprioception is:
o: The body's ability to sense its general orientation and the relative position of all its parts
The speed of a nerve impulse
e: Training proprioceptive ability improves balance, coordination and posture, and lets the body adapt to its surroundings without conscious thought.

q: Which division produces the fight-or-flight response?
e: Sympathetic increases neural activity, signals endocrine organs to release hormones such as adrenaline, and raises heart rate, breathing and alertness. Parasympathetic is rest and digest.

q: A client is just learning a skill and performance is inconsistent. Which stage is this, and what should the trainer do?
o: Associative; refine through practice and feedback
Cognitive; use simple instructions and break the skill into smaller steps
e: The three stages are cognitive, associative and autonomous. Associative gets practice and regular feedback; autonomous gets new versions to further challenge them.

q: Bioenergetics is:
o: The study of energy in the human body: how chemical energy from food is converted into mechanical energy
The sum of the three energy systems
e: Energy is the capacity to do work. Bioenergetics is the study of how food's chemical energy becomes mechanical energy.

q: Which side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood, and where does it pump it?
e: The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs. The left receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the entire body.

q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
o: It pumps under higher pressure over a greater distance, to the whole body
e: The right ventricle pumps under low pressure only a short distance to the lungs, so its wall is thin.

q: Which structure is the pacemaker of the heart?
o: The SA node in the right atrium
e: The SA node initiates the signal. Internodal pathways carry it to the AV node, which delays it so the ventricles can fill before contracting. The result is normal sinus rhythm.

q: Why does the AV node delay the impulse?
o: To slow the heart rate overall
To allow the ventricles to fill with blood from the atria before contracting
e: The delay is what makes filling possible, producing an effective stroke volume.

q: Blood makes up approximately what proportion of total body weight?
e: About 8 percent, roughly 5 litres in the average person, and it is thicker and heavier than water.

q: Which blood cells contain growth factors that may help healing after injury?
e: Platelets assist with clotting and contain growth factors. Those factors assist vasculogenesis, the formation of new capillaries, and angiogenesis, formation of new capillaries from existing vessels.

q: Which vessels are the exchange sites of water and chemicals between blood and tissues?
e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries are the smallest vessels and the exchange sites.

q: In capillary exchange, which substances only exit into the tissues?
e: Water both enters and exits, carbon dioxide only enters from the tissues, and glucose and oxygen only exit into the tissues.

q: Which are the primary respiratory muscles used in quiet breathing?
e: Quiet inspiration uses the diaphragm and external intercostals. Heavy or forced breathing additionally recruits the secondary muscles: scalenes, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor.

q: In quiet breathing, expiration is:
o: Passive, from relaxation of the inspiratory muscles
e: Inspiration is always active: contracting the inspiratory muscles increases thoracic volume and drops intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric, drawing air in. Quiet expiration is passive.

q: Normal respiratory rate at rest is:
e: 12 to 16 at rest. Tachypnea is above 24, bradypnea below 8.

q: Where does gas exchange with the bloodstream take place?
e: Alveoli sit in clusters of alveolar sacs at the end of the bronchioles, surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses across the capillary membranes into the blood.

q: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the heart through the:
o: Pulmonary arteries, into the right atrium
Pulmonary veins, into the left atrium
Vena cava, into the right ventricle
e: Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries; oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, then out to the tissues.

q: The conducting airways do more than carry air. What else do they do?
o: Purify, humidify, and warm or cool the air to match body temperature
e: The nasal and oral cavities, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchioles gather and condition the air. The respiratory system also filters the 7,000 to 9,000 litres breathed daily.

q: Efficient oxygen uptake depends on three things. Which is NOT one of them?
o: The respiratory system's ability to collect oxygen
The cardiovascular system's ability to absorb and transport it
The tissues' ability to use it
The kidneys' ability to filter it
e: Collect, transport, use. Those three determine efficient oxygen uptake.

q: Aside from surgery, how is mass physically removed from the body?
o: Through the carbon dioxide exhaled with every breath
e: We are carbon-based, so exhaled carbon dioxide is the route out. Related point: fat cannot be burned without the presence of oxygen.

q: A client shows a rapid shallow upper-chest breathing pattern. What should you do?
o: Correct it yourself with breathing drills only
Refer them to a medical professional; teaching correct breathing remains within scope
Ignore it, as it is outside scope entirely
e: Refer for the abnormal pattern. Teaching correct breathing is within scope. Consequences of the pattern include dizziness, anxiety, fatigue, poor sleep and poor circulation.

q: Which two energy pathways are anaerobic?
e: ATP-PCr and glycolysis do not require oxygen. The oxidative pathway is aerobic. Together the three form the bioenergetic continuum.

q: Which system is activated at the onset of any activity, regardless of intensity?
o: None; it depends entirely on intensity
e: ATP-PCr produces energy fastest, so it starts everything, then sustains only about 10 seconds before another system takes over.

q: How much energy does the creatine phosphate reaction release for muscle contraction?
e: Creatine phosphate plus ADP yields creatine plus ATP, releasing 7.3 kcals. ATP and PCr are phosphagens, hence the alternative name, the phosphagen system.

q: At what intensity does the ATP-PCr system predominate?
e: 90 to 100 percent: power and strength training with heavy loads and few repetitions, or short sprinting.

q: How many ATP does one glucose molecule produce through anaerobic glycolysis?
e: Two ATP, with pyruvate as a by-product. If the cell cannot use pyruvate fast enough, lactic acid builds up, increasing cell acidity, interfering with contraction and decreasing performance.

q: A typical set of 8 to 12 repetitions primarily stresses which system?
e: Glycolysis covers moderate to high intensity for roughly 30 to 60 seconds, and a typical 8 to 12 rep range falls inside that window.

q: What distinguishes fast glycolysis from slow glycolysis?
o: Fast is aerobic, slow is anaerobic
Fast is anaerobic at 80 to 90 percent intensity for one to two minutes; slow is aerobic and needs lower intensity
Fast uses fat, slow uses carbohydrate
Fast produces more ATP per glucose
e: Fast glycolysis breaks down glucose without oxygen and delivers energy quickly. Slow glycolysis uses oxygen and is a slower process, which is why intensity must come down to use it.

q: How many ATP does one glucose molecule yield through the oxidative system?
o: 36, and up to 38 depending on substrates and pathways
e: 36 ATP, up to 38. With oxygen present, pyruvate is not converted to lactic acid and instead becomes a substrate for ATP production.

q: Why is the oxidative system the slowest to produce energy?
o: It uses fat, which is hard to break down
It needs oxygen in amounts matching the muscular requirement, and elevating respiration takes time
e: It is the slowest but produces the most. It becomes more involved beyond 30 seconds and is predominant beyond 2 minutes.

q: Fat, carbohydrate and protein enter the oxidative system by different routes. Where do they converge?
e: Fat becomes free fatty acids then beta-oxidation; carbohydrate becomes glucose then glycolysis then pyruvate; protein becomes amino acids then deamination. All converge on acetyl-CoA, then the citric acid cycle, then the electron transport chain.

q: At lower intensity levels there is a primary reliance on:
e: The oxidative system covers long endurance activities and also working, standing and sitting, making it the primary energy system for the majority of daily life.

q: What is the relationship between intensity and duration?
o: Inverse: as intensity goes up, duration must come down
It depends on the client's fitness
e: Intensity and duration have an inverse relationship. That, plus the fact that all three systems keep working while one predominates, are the two governing principles.

q: When one energy system is predominant, what are the others doing?
o: Still working, recovering and preparing for when they are called on again
Being inhibited by the nervous system
e: They are not providing the majority of the energy, but they are active and recovering.

q: Which training approach best develops the glycolytic system?
o: Interval training balancing exercise with short recovery periods
Short-duration high-intensity work with long rests
e: ATP-PCr wants short high-intensity work with adequate rest for phosphocreatine recovery. Oxidative wants long-duration moderate-intensity work. Glycolysis wants intervals with short recoveries.
